subject: Number of Beth-shemeshites struck down for looking into the Ark

figures.name: Men of Beth-shemesh struck down
figures.note: MT reads 'seventy men, fifty thousand men'; LXX (Vaticanus) reads only 'seventy men'; SP does not contain 1 Samuel (Samuel is outside the Pentateuch), so no SP reading exists.

systematic_analysis.pattern: The divergence is not part of a systematic numerical scheme but appears to be an isolated textual problem. The MT awkwardly juxtaposes 'seventy men' and 'fifty thousand men' without a connecting waw in some witnesses and with reversed numerical order (smaller before larger), violating standard Hebrew syntax. Several Hebrew manuscripts, Josephus (Ant. 6.16), and the LXX preserve only 'seventy,' suggesting '50,000' is a secondary intrusion rather than a deliberate inflation pattern.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: Unlike the patriarchal chronologies, this is a one-off textual oddity rather than a system. The Hebrew text gives an enormous and grammatically strange number (50,070), while the Greek and Josephus give just 70.

theories.name: Scribal error / glossatorial intrusion
theories.summary: The most widely held view (S. R. Driver, McCarter, Tsumura) is that 'fifty thousand men' is a secondary marginal gloss or numerical corruption that entered the MT, since the syntax is anomalous (smaller number precedes larger, contrary to Hebrew convention) and Beth-shemesh, a small village, could not plausibly contain 50,000 men. The shorter LXX reading ('seventy') and Josephus's '70' likely preserve the original.
theories.summary_plain: Scholars think a scribe accidentally added '50,000' to the original number of 70, since the Hebrew grammar is broken and the village was far too small to have that many men.
supporting_evidence: The word order 'seventy men, fifty thousand men' violates standard Hebrew numerical syntax which places larger numbers first.
Several medieval Hebrew manuscripts (noted by Kennicott) omit '50,000 men' entirely.
LXX Vaticanus and Josephus (Antiquities 6.16) read only seventy.
Beth-shemesh was a small Levitical town incapable of supporting a population of 50,000 adult males.
The Targum and rabbinic tradition felt the difficulty and reinterpreted the number (e.g., '70 men, each equal to 50,000').
weaknesses: No extant Hebrew manuscript actually preserves a clean text without the gloss as the primary reading.
The mechanism by which '50,000' entered remains speculative — whether marginal note, dittography, or numerical siglum misread.

theories.name: MT inflation / theological amplification
theories.summary: A minority view holds that the MT tradition inflated the casualty figure to magnify the holiness of the Ark and the gravity of its violation, paralleling other large-number expansions in Samuel-Kings. This would make the divergence a theologically motivated emphasis on divine judgment.
theories.summary_plain: Some suggest the larger number was added on purpose to dramatize how holy the Ark was and how serious the offense.
supporting_evidence: Other passages in MT Samuel show numerical inflation versus LXX (e.g., 1 Sam 13:5 chariots).
Theological emphasis on Ark holiness pervades 1 Samuel 4–6.
Rabbinic interpretive tradition leans into the magnitude of the slaughter.
weaknesses: The grammatical awkwardness suggests accident rather than deliberate composition.
No coherent theological motive explains the bizarre word order.
Josephus, working from a Hebrew-like Vorlage, knew only 70.

theories.name: LXX deflation / abbreviation
theories.summary: An inverse possibility is that the LXX shortened or rationalized an original large MT number because 50,070 seemed implausible. This would make the MT primary and LXX a corrective abridgment.
theories.summary_plain: Possibly the Greek translators dropped the huge number because it seemed unrealistic.
supporting_evidence: LXX translators occasionally rationalize implausible figures.
MT is generally the lectio difficilior here.
weaknesses: Josephus independently attests '70,' suggesting a Hebrew Vorlage without 50,000.
The MT's syntactic anomaly is better explained as corruption than as the original.
LXX rarely deletes numbers wholesale without trace.

theories.name: Independent textual traditions
theories.summary: The divergence may reflect two genuinely distinct textual streams (proto-MT and the Vorlage of LXX), with the Qumran Samuel scrolls demonstrating substantial pluriformity in Samuel's text. The shorter and longer readings could descend from parallel ancient editions.
theories.summary_plain: The Hebrew and Greek versions of Samuel come from different ancient editions, so the difference may simply reflect two old traditions.
supporting_evidence: 4QSamuel-a shows the LXX often reflects a different, sometimes superior Hebrew Vorlage.
Samuel is one of the most textually pluriform books of the Hebrew Bible.
Multiple ancient versions diverge on this verse.
weaknesses: 1 Samuel 6:19 is not extant in the Qumran Samuel fragments, so direct evidence is lacking.
The MT's internal grammatical problem still points to corruption rather than a clean alternative edition.

overall_assessment: The textual problem at 1 Samuel 6:19 is best explained as an accidental corruption or marginal gloss in the proto-MT tradition, where '50,000 men' intruded into an original reading of 'seventy men' preserved by the LXX and Josephus. The anomalous Hebrew syntax (smaller number preceding larger) is the decisive evidence, since deliberate composition would not produce such a malformed phrase. This case illustrates that not every MT–LXX numerical divergence reflects a systematic ideological program (as in the Genesis 5/11 chronologies); some are simply transmission accidents. The verse is a textbook example of the value of LXX and Josephus as witnesses to a pre-MT Hebrew text.
overall_plain: The Hebrew Bible's '50,070' is almost certainly a scribal accident; the original number was probably just '70,' as preserved in the Greek translation and in Josephus. This shows that ancient versions sometimes preserve better readings than the standard Hebrew text.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Broken syntax betrays an ancient scribal intrusion
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The malformed word order in MT 1 Samuel 6:19 is one of the clearest cases in the Hebrew Bible where grammatical evidence alone reveals textual corruption, independent of versional comparison. That the LXX and Josephus converge on the cleaner reading vindicates the methodological principle that the MT, while generally reliable, requires correction at specific points where internal evidence and ancient witnesses concur. This passage cautions against treating all numerical divergences as ideologically driven systems.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The strange Hebrew grammar of this verse is itself proof that something went wrong in copying. The Greek Bible and Josephus help us recover what the original probably said.
